newsitem.title: UK: No reprieve for low-yielding Japanese bonds.
newsitem.headline: No reprieve for low-yielding Japanese bonds.

text.p: Japanese investors, frustrated with the meagre yield on domestic government bonds (JGBs), will continue look to markets further afield for higher returns, analysts said on Thursday.

But for those investors restricted to the domestic currency, yen Eurobonds offer a profitable alternative, they said. Japanese general elections on Sunday are not likely to have a big impact on the market, with no change of economic policy expected, analysts said.
"Japanese bonds yields are very low indeed and this is forcing Japanese institutions to increase their overseas investment," said Stuart Thomson, at Nikko (Europe) in London.
"The weakness of the yen against all major currencies in the last few periods is evidence that investors are increasing their overseas weighting," said Thomson, Nikko's chief international economist.
He said the major markets to benefit from this investor flow were U.S. Treasuries, high-yielding European government bonds and traditional favourites like Australian and Canadian bonds.
"Investor perference is shifting away from JGBs in an international environment where the upside is still there for the U.S. market," said Julian Fisher, economist at Daiwa Europe in London.
He said fears of a rise in U.S. interest rates in the near future had somewhat abated and Treasuries respresented a safe haven for now.
But Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International in London, noted that many Japanese investors were not able to invest in foreign currencies or were wary of doing so.
"One way to get high-yielding yen assets is through Euroyen," said Hannah. "This is a favoured approach with no currency risk but buying a slightly lesser credit name."
A lot of slightly lesser rated sovereigns had issued in yen giving reasonable spreads over JGBs, he said.

Hannah said a second alternative, whereby investors took only a partial currency risk, was to buy dual currency bonds. Here the principle or coupon is paid in yen but the other element is paid in a foreign currency, "so you are taking a bit of risk but not going the whole hog."
Some analysts said JGB yields could improve in the not too distant future, with the Japanese economic outlook less bleak than it was a year ago.

"JGB yield levels are close to where they were in October 1995 but the fundamentals stand in stark contrast," said Fisher. "In 1995 the threat to the financial sector seemed much greater than it does now."

"As evidence gathers that the economy is increasingly driven by a sustainable private sector recovery, characterised by rising investment and consumer spending, then yield levels will begin to rise over the course of the next quarter," he said.
IBJ's Hannah also said there was a positive side for JGBs with the demand/supply balance favourable to domestic bonds.

"The bond market could still actually perform quiet well," he said. "There will be some hesitation to push yields below 2.5 percent but the bond market can still rally from here. There is nothing to prevent that from happening."

The elections were not expected to result in any major market disruption, with the two most expected results -- either an outright majority for the ruling LDP party or a centre right coalition with the LDP as the senior partner -- already priced into the market, analysts said.
